Ultraviolet damage and erythema

A 15-person self-controlled study found more than 50% less UVB erythema on at least one test occasion in 85% of participants after red-light pretreatment. Animal and cell studies often found reduced UV injury, although one high-dose near-infrared protocol worsened damage.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A 15-person self-controlled study found more than 50% less UVB erythema on at least one test occasion in 85% of participants after red-light pretreatment. Animal and cell studies often found reduced UV injury, although one high-dose near-infrared protocol worsened damage.

Summary of the Evidence

Twenty publications address ultraviolet-related skin damage or erythema: one small human nonrandomized study, six animal studies, twelve in-vitro studies, and one letter. This count includes different exposure timings and laboratory models, not twenty clinical trials. Two mouse publications combine PBM with Lycium-derived products, so the effects of the light cannot be isolated completely in those experiments.

Human and clinical evidence

A self-controlled pilot studied 13 healthy participants and two people with polymorphous light eruption. After five, six, or ten pretreatment sessions with 660-nm red LED, UVB erythema was reduced by more than 50% on at least one test occasion in 85% of participants. The authors also reported an SPF-15-like response and less post-inflammatory pigmentation on treated skin. This is a direct favorable result for short-term erythema after pretreatment, but the study did not randomize or blind participants and did not evaluate long-term protection from skin cancer or chronic photoaging (Barolet and Boucher 2008).

Animal evidence

Most of the six mouse and rat studies report less epidermal thickening, collagen disruption, or other UV-related injury when red or near-infrared light was given before or after UV exposure. One rat study found greater skin damage after a high-dose near-infrared protocol following UV exposure. Pretreatment and post-exposure treatment answer different questions, and the direction of effect is not uniform across all settings.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

The twelve cell studies commonly report lower reactive oxygen species, inflammatory mediators, or matrix-degrading activity, along with changes in DNA-repair or collagen measures. Wavelength, dose, timing, and temperature vary, and the results are not all protective. No separate ex-vivo clinical-tissue series was identified in the category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The human study used pulsed 660-nm red visible light at 60 mW/cm² and 5 J/cm², delivered in five to ten sessions over one to three weeks before UV exposure. Animal and cell protocols span multiple visible and near-infrared wavelengths and different timing relative to UV. There is no head-to-head dose study defining a clinical pretreatment schedule, and laboratory photoprotection should not be treated as a replacement for established sun protection.

Interpretation

The human pilot found less acute UVB redness after red-light pretreatment, while preclinical studies often found reduced tissue injury. The adverse result in one high-dose animal protocol shows that the direction depends on exposure conditions. These findings concern short-term responses to experimental UV, not demonstrated prevention of long-term skin disease.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term reduction of UVB erythema after red-light pretreatment Low-to-moderate for selected preclinical skin-protection outcomes
Publications and records20 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One small self-controlled human study found less UVB erythema after red-light pretreatment, and several animal and cell studies report reduced tissue injury or stress markers. A high-dose near-infrared animal experiment found worse injury, showing that protocols matter. Larger randomized human studies with independent replication and longer-term outcomes would support a stronger clinical conclusion.
